note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: May the input be modified, and is O(1) extra space a hard requirement?
What is the answer for an empty list?
Can values be negative or larger than n - 1?
hints: A permutation of 0..n-1 has every value inside the range and no repeats.
Value v belongs at index v: placing values into their own slots needs no extra table.
Swap nums[i] into slot nums[i] until slot i holds i; an out-of-range value or a slot already holding its own value means failure.
invariants: after processing index i, every slot j <= i that is reached holds j
each swap fixes one value permanently, so there are at most n swaps
chooseWhen: A membership test must not allocate a second table (when mutation is allowed)
tradeoffs: Cyclic placement needs a writable array; without mutation a copy (or a boolean table) costs O(n) memory

clarifyingQuestions: How do Shuffle Mode and Random Mode differ exactly?
Is the playlist size known, and are songs numbered?
May the observation start in the middle of a shuffle cycle?
Does a new cycle reshuffle independently of the previous one?
hints: Only repeats matter: two plays of the same song must be separated by a cycle boundary.
Consecutive plays of one song at distance numSongs or more always have a boundary between them.
Each close repeat allows a contiguous arc of boundary offsets mod numSongs; intersect all arcs with a difference array.
invariants: a piece never contains a song twice
if consecutive occurrences of every song are separated, all occurrences are
chooseWhen: Long observation windows where testing every offset would be quadratic
tradeoffs: The difference array costs O(numSongs) memory even for short sequences; a sorted list of arcs would avoid that
hack2hire:68ad8c5bcdaebe9459ce9a7f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: shuffle-cycle consistency with an unknown starting offset

clarifyingQuestions: Should the average be a floating-point value, rounded, or floored?
When equal values tie for the k-th largest, how many are removed?
Can k equal windowSize?
hints: Average of the rest = (window sum - sum of the k largest) / (windowSize - k).
Keep the k largest in one heap and the others in a second heap, each with a running sum.
Delete lazily: tag each entry with its index and skip entries that left the window or moved to the other heap.
invariants: the top heap holds exactly the k largest (value, index) pairs of the window
topSum + restSum equals the window sum
chooseWhen: Large windows where re-sorting every window is too slow
tradeoffs: Lazy heaps keep stale entries until they surface, so memory is O(n) rather than O(windowSize)
hack2hire:67886e3c402dc47b67a14940.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: floored sliding-window averages without the k largest

clarifyingQuestions: Where do the per-plan prices come from, and in what unit?
Are input and output tokens priced differently?
How should the result be ordered and formatted?
hints: Parse every comma-separated row exactly once.
Look prices up in a hash map keyed by plan.
Accumulate totals per user in a hash map, then sort the user ids for output.
invariants: every total is the sum of its sessions' costs
each user appears once in the output
chooseWhen: Many sessions, few plans
tradeoffs: A hash map plus a final sort is simple; keeping users ordered while scanning is unnecessary
hack2hire:6a1a06bfc81f779dc6a23737.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: per-token pricing per plan

clarifyingQuestions: Is the fee charged per user, per plan, or per (user, plan)?
Are free tokens shared by input and output, and which is consumed first?
Are sessions processed in list order?
hints: Keep a remaining-allowance counter per (user, plan).
Within a session, take free input tokens first, then free output tokens.
Add the monthly fee the first time a (user, plan) pair appears.
invariants: remaining allowance never goes below 0
a pair pays the fee exactly once
chooseWhen: Billing with allowances that depend on session order
tradeoffs: Keying by (user, plan) costs memory per pair; a per-user nested map is equivalent
hack2hire:6a1a06e9c81f779dc6a2373a.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: monthly fee and included tokens per plan

clarifyingQuestions: Does the cap include the monthly fee?
Is the cap per plan or per user across plans?
Do free tokens still apply under a cap?
hints: Track uncapped usage per (user, plan); the cap applies to the pair's whole month.
Apply min(cap, usage) only after all sessions are processed.
Add the fee outside the cap and sum the pairs per user.
invariants: each pair's charge is at most monthly_fee + usage_cap
totals are sums of non-negative integers
chooseWhen: Monthly caps that apply to accumulated usage
tradeoffs: Capping at the end is simplest; capping incrementally would allow early exit but gives the same result
hack2hire:6a1a0712c81f779dc6a2373b.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: monthly usage cap per plan

constraints: paths have at most 20 segments of [a-z0-9]{1,10}
clarifyingQuestions: Is a prefix measured in whole segments or in characters?
Is "/" registrable, and is it an ancestor of every path?
Are wildcards or path parameters supported?
Does an exact match count as its own closest ancestor?
hints: Paths are sequences of segments, so a trie of segments fits naturally.
While walking the query, remember the last node that had a handler.
Registering overwrites the handler at the node for that exact path.
invariants: a node has a handler only if that exact path was registered
the returned handler belongs to the deepest registered node on the query path
chooseWhen: Many lookups against a growing set of route prefixes
tradeoffs: A hash map of every registered path and a scan over the query prefixes is simpler but rebuilds prefix strings per lookup
hack2hire:6862f418eb0810914237ab13.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest registered ancestor lookup

constraints: phones match [0-9 ()+-]{1,20} with at least one digit
clarifyingQuestions: What should be returned: duplicate indices, registered names, or a count?
Are emails compared case-insensitively or normalised?
Do failed accounts claim their email or phone?
hints: Process accounts strictly in order; only registered accounts claim identifiers.
Keep claimed emails and claimed phones in two hash sets.
An account is a duplicate if either identifier is already in its set.
invariants: claimed sets contain identifiers of registered accounts only
duplicate indices are ascending
chooseWhen: Streaming deduplication on two keys
tradeoffs: Two sets are enough because a duplicate never claims anything; union-find is not needed
hack2hire:69fe5a7f574d87bc4900687d.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: duplicates by exact email or phone

constraints: phones match [0-9 ()+-]{1,20} with at least one digit
clarifyingQuestions: Which email rules apply: case, dots, "+" tags, and only for some providers?
Are phone country codes significant?
Is the part after "@" also normalised?
hints: Write one normalisation function per identifier and apply it once per account.
Cut the local part at the first "+" before removing dots.
Then deduplicate exactly as in level 1 with the normalised keys.
invariants: two accounts conflict exactly when a normalised identifier is equal
duplicate indices are ascending
chooseWhen: Identifiers with many equivalent spellings
tradeoffs: Fixed normalisation rules are fast but must match the product's real equivalence; a provider-specific table would be more precise
hack2hire:69fe5a9a574d87bc4900687e.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: duplicates after email and phone normalisation

clarifyingQuestions: What are the constructor parameters and the method name?
Is time implicit (one call per second) or passed in?
Do rejected requests count toward the limit?
Is the window half-open?
hints: The clock is the call counter, so keep it inside the object.
Each domain needs only the times of its accepted requests that are still inside the window.
A deque per domain: drop old times from the front, append the new time when accepting.
invariants: each deque holds at most maxRequests times
times in a deque are strictly increasing
chooseWhen: Per-key sliding windows with frequent calls
tradeoffs: A deque per domain keeps up to maxRequests times; a fixed ring buffer would bound memory per domain more tightly
hack2hire:6a7a3b72d713d873ca7aaf62.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: per-domain sliding-window limit with implicit one-second clock

constraints: 0 <= n <= 1e5, masses and speeds have equal length
clarifyingQuestions: Which quantity decides a collision: mass, speed, or momentum?
Can a faster asteroid catch one moving the same way?
Does the survivor lose mass or speed?
What is the output format?
hints: Only a right-mover followed by a left-mover can meet; a stack holds the survivors so far.
Compare momenta mass * |speed|; the larger survives unchanged.
A new left-mover keeps fighting the stack top while the top moves right.
invariants: the stack never has a right-mover directly below a left-mover
momentum comparisons are exact integers below 2**53
chooseWhen: Collision chains that cascade through many asteroids
tradeoffs: The stack gives O(n) but assumes no overtaking; a time-ordered event simulation would be needed if same-direction asteroids could meet
hack2hire:679dc578996c3c60bd38b5bc.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: 735-style collisions decided by momentum

clarifyingQuestions: In which order should matches be returned?
Are duplicate words returned more than once?
Does a word identical to the query count as its anagram?
hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when their sorted letters are equal.
Group the words by that signature once, before answering queries.
Each query is then one hash lookup; copy the list so answers do not share containers.
invariants: every returned word has the query's signature
matches keep the input order of words
chooseWhen: Many queries over a fixed word list
tradeoffs: Sorted-letter keys cost O(L log L) per word; 26-count keys are O(L) but longer to hash
hack2hire:6a9748740ca9cc4e1c789f00.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: anagram lookup per query

clarifyingQuestions: Can balls be taken from both ends, or only from the front?
May a player take one ball from each end in a single turn?
Should we return a win flag, the first player's score, or the difference?
Is a tie a win for the first player?
hints: Because the total is fixed, maximising your own score is maximising the difference to the opponent.
The state is the remaining interval [l, r]; the mover chooses one of four moves.
diff(l, r) = max over moves of (taken sum - diff(remaining interval)); compute intervals by increasing length.
invariants: diff of an empty interval is 0
first score = (total + diff(0, n-1)) / 2 is an integer
chooseWhen: Two-player zero-sum games on a shrinking line
tradeoffs: Interval DP is O(n^2); a front-only variant would be O(n), so the allowed ends decide the cost
hack2hire:67775b978df5ec401f786db0.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: two-end take-one-or-two game

constraints: dates match YYYY-MM-DD with month 01-12 and day 01-31
clarifyingQuestions: What should be returned for each country: the date only, or also the attendees?
What happens to a country with no available dates?
Can a participant list the same date twice?
How should countries be ordered?
hints: Group by country, then count dates within the country.
Because "YYYY-MM-DD" strings sort chronologically, the earliest date is the smallest string.
After picking the date, a second pass collects the attendees in input order.
invariants: each country appears at most once
every attendee is available on the chosen date
chooseWhen: Group-by then arg-max with a tie rule
tradeoffs: Two passes over participants are simple; storing attendee lists per date would avoid the second pass but uses more memory
hack2hire:6965d17bd0c1ba0f117959a2.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: most-available date per country with attendees

clarifyingQuestions: What exactly triggers an explosion?
Do bubbles fall after an explosion, and in which direction?
Does the process repeat until stable?
Should the result be a new matrix or the input modified?
hints: Mark first, remove after: explosions in one round are simultaneous.
A bubble with two or more same-colored neighbours marks itself and those neighbours.
Apply gravity per column with a write pointer from the bottom, then repeat until no cell is marked.
invariants: each round removes at least three bubbles or ends the process
after gravity no empty cell lies below a bubble in its column
chooseWhen: Small boards with cascading simulation
tradeoffs: Full rescans per round are simple; tracking only cells near the previous changes would be faster on large boards
hack2hire:6a7fc7a7d713d873ca7ade7b.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: repeated neighbour-triggered explosions with gravity

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned when every digit is 0?
May the result have a leading zero?
Is the input ever empty?
hints: With a fixed number of digits, the smallest number is the lexicographically smallest valid digit string.
The first digit must be the smallest non-zero digit.
After it, all remaining digits go in increasing order, zeros first; counting digits is enough.
invariants: the result uses every digit exactly once (except the all-zero case)
the first character is not "0" unless the result is "0"
chooseWhen: Small alphabets where counting replaces sorting
tradeoffs: Counting sort is O(n); a general sort is simpler to write but O(n log n)
hack2hire:68dd8441fb98b196fa54054b.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: smallest number from single digits

clarifyingQuestions: Are elements single digits or whole numbers?
What if the comparator-smallest arrangement starts with 0?
What is returned when every element is 0?
hints: All arrangements have the same length, so compare them as strings.
Without zeros, sorting by a + b < b + a gives the smallest concatenation.
With zeros, the first element must be non-zero; try each distinct non-zero value first and sort the rest by the comparator.
invariants: every candidate uses each element exactly once
the result does not start with "0" unless it is "0"
chooseWhen: Concatenation order problems with a leading-zero restriction
tradeoffs: Trying every distinct first element costs O(distinct * total digits); a sharper rule for the first element would avoid it but is easy to get wrong (the comparator-smallest non-zero element is not always best)
hack2hire:68dd8827fb98b196fa54054e.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: smallest concatenation of whole numbers

clarifyingQuestions: Must both sides be non-empty?
Is a single element a spike?
Can a value appear on both sides of the peak?
hints: Each side is strictly monotone, so a value can appear at most once per side.
Choosing the largest value as the peak never hurts.
Every smaller value can appear twice (once per side); the peak only once.
invariants: the answer is at most 2 * distinct - 1
the answer is at least 1 for non-empty input
chooseWhen: Counting arguments replace construction
tradeoffs: A hash map counts in O(n); sorting first is also fine at O(n log n)
hack2hire:67d842e41989183df53824ed.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximum spike length

constraints: logs are well nested and every task is closed
clarifyingQuestions: What should be computed: exclusive time, inclusive time, or the busiest task?
Is an exit timestamp inclusive or exclusive?
Can the same task name be entered again, even nested?
hints: A single CPU runs only the innermost open task.
Charge the time since the previous event to the task on top of the stack before handling the new event.
Push on enter, pop on exit; sum the charges per name.
invariants: the stack holds the open tasks innermost last
the exclusive times sum to (last - first) minus idle time
chooseWhen: Nested intervals sharing one resource
tradeoffs: Half-open time makes nested charges add up exactly; inclusive ends need +1 adjustments
hack2hire:6787150fe20f8f324213c295.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: exclusive CPU time per task

constraints: message characters are printable ASCII (space to ~)
clarifyingQuestions: Should we encode, decode, or find the rotation?
Is case preserved?
What happens to digits and punctuation?
Can the shift be negative or larger than 26?
hints: Only the shift modulo 26 matters; normalise it to 0..25 even for negative values.
Upper- and lower-case letters rotate within their own alphabets.
Precompute a translation table once and map every character through it.
invariants: non-letters are unchanged
a shift of 26 * k leaves the message unchanged
chooseWhen: Character-wise substitutions over a small alphabet
tradeoffs: A translation table costs a few hundred bytes and avoids per-character arithmetic
hack2hire:699f73ca6e73e4abccc9b540.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: Caesar encoding with any integer shift
